question: In nuclear energy, what is the primary commercial bottleneck preventing utilities from deploying small modular reactors at scale?
guest: There are 96 OEMs claiming to manufacture small modular reactors—probably more today. We've focused on commercial and technical feasibility and culled that down to three or four that we think might be viable going forward. But here's the issue on small modular reactors: who's going to take the last-dollar risk? You don't know what the end cost is going to be. We're not going to put that on our customers, and it has to be sensible for our shareholders—we're not going to take uncapped risk on behalf of our shareholders. Maybe we'll put a little bit at risk, not much, and it has to be capped. So you have to bring a number of different wallets together. The hyperscaler, if that's your customer, would have to take some risk. The EPC contractor would have to take some risk. The OEM, whose technology it is, should ultimately take the risk, but many times they're undercapitalized and can't, so there's a limit on how much they can actually take. Having the federal government come in and help out is going to be an important part of who takes last-dollar risk.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The main bottleneck is economic: first-of-a-kind cost and financing risk. SMRs are supposed to become cheap through factory-built repetition, but those savings only appear once a vendor has a deep order book, and utilities will not place firm orders until someone else has shown a unit can be built on budget and on schedule. The result is a standoff in which no one wants to pay for the first few units.

The clearest illustration is NuScale's Carbon Free Power Project in Utah, cancelled in November 2023 after its target power price rose from about $58 to $89 per MWh and too few utilities subscribed. Regulated utilities and their commissions are also wary after the Vogtle overruns, so the cost-overrun risk has no willing owner without government backstops or large customers such as data-centre operators underwriting it.

Other constraints are real but secondary: licensing timelines, limited supply of HALEU fuel for many advanced designs, and an immature supply chain and workforce. These mostly feed back into the same problem, which is uncertain delivered cost per MWh compared with gas, renewables and storage.

This is from my own knowledge rather than a fresh search, so developments from the last several months may not be reflected.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
The primary commercial bottleneck preventing utilities from deploying small modular reactors at scale is the first-of-a-kind (FOAK) cost and risk impasse—an orderbook chicken-and-egg dilemma. Unlike conventional gigawatt reactors that rely on physical economies of size, SMRs depend on economies of volume: serial factory fabrication, standardized licensing, and repeatable modular construction across a committed orderbook of at least five to ten identical units. Until that manufacturing pipeline exists, early units remain bespoke builds carrying steep capital costs, schedule uncertainty, and overrun risk, as seen in the canceled NuScale-UAMPS project.

Regulated utilities, bound by strict ratepayer-protection mandates and regulatory prudency reviews, cannot easily justify absorbing unquantified FOAK premiums when moving first mainly subsidizes the learning curve for later buyers, especially while competing designs fragment early demand. Conversely, reactor vendors and specialized fuel suppliers cannot finance dedicated factories and HALEU fuel infrastructure without firm multi-unit orders. Breaking this deadlock requires multi-buyer consortia, government cost-overrun backstops, or deep-pocketed hyperscale data center off-takers willing to underwrite initial deployments until nth-of-a-kind cost certainty is proven.

noweb.answer: The primary commercial bottleneck preventing utilities from deploying small modular reactors at scale is a classic chicken-and-egg dilemma around first-of-a-kind cost and construction risk. Unlike conventional gigawatt plants that rely on size for efficiency, SMRs depend on factory mass production and standardized learning curves to achieve competitive economics. However, vendors cannot justify investing billions in dedicated manufacturing lines and specialized supply chains—including high-assay low-enriched uranium fuel for advanced designs—without a deep, binding orderbook. Conversely, risk-averse utilities and their regulators are reluctant to commit ratepayer capital until an operating commercial unit proves it can be delivered on schedule and on budget, a hesitation reinforced by high-profile project cancellations over escalating material and financing costs. Because initial units must absorb steep upfront licensing, engineering, and bespoke fabrication expenses without factory economies of volume, their electricity looks far costlier per megawatt-hour than natural gas or renewables. Ultimately, almost every utility wants the proven economics of buying the tenth reactor off an assembly line, leaving virtually none willing to bear the open-ended financial risk of building the first.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main bottleneck is **first-of-a-kind cost and risk**, which leaves vendors without an order book.

SMRs are supposed to get cheap through factory-style series production. That only happens after many units have been built. No utility wants to be the first buyer and absorb the uncertain construction costs, the risk of overruns, and the regulatory risk that come with early units. Without firm orders, vendors can't build supply chains or move down the learning curve. Without that, prices stay high, and orders stay scarce. NuScale's project with Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems shows how this plays out. It was cancelled in 2023 after its estimated power price rose to about $89/MWh. Subscribers walked away even with large federal subsidies.

Other constraints make the problem worse. These include limited supply of the high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) that many advanced designs need, licensing timelines, and gaps in the specialized supply chain and workforce. All of them come back to the same problem: utilities and their regulators won't commit capital until someone else proves costs on real, delivered units. That's why recent momentum depends on government cost-sharing and power purchase agreements from tech companies, which absorb some of that early risk.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: The primary commercial bottleneck is the first-of-a-kind (FOAK) capital cost and financing trap, which creates a classic chicken-and-egg problem. Because SMRs give up the traditional economies of scale that lower per-megawatt costs in large nuclear plants, their business case depends on "economies of multiples"—standardized, factory-based mass manufacturing and repeated construction learning curves. However, utilities are reluctant to absorb the steep upfront capital costs, high financing rates, and cost-overrun risks of building the first several units when those early reactors produce electricity far more expensively than natural gas or renewables paired with storage. Without firm, multi-unit orderbooks, developers cannot justify investing in dedicated manufacturing facilities or specialized supply chains (such as HALEU fuel for advanced designs), keeping unit prices high and schedules long. Compounded by lengthy, design-specific regulatory licensing, this risk gap leaves utilities waiting for proven, nth-of-a-kind pricing before committing—stalling the very deployments needed to achieve it.

noweb.answer: The primary commercial bottleneck is the first-of-a-kind cost trap, often described as an orderbook chicken-and-egg problem. Because small modular reactors forfeit the traditional economies of scale that make large reactors cheaper per megawatt, their business case depends on "economies of multiples"—standardized factory manufacturing and repeat construction to drive down unit costs. However, building dedicated factories, qualifying supply chains (such as specialized fuels like HALEU), and navigating lengthy licensing processes require massive upfront capital. Risk-averse regulated utilities, scarred by past nuclear cost overruns and able to buy cheaper renewables, storage, or natural gas, are unwilling to absorb the high price and financial risk of early units. Without firm, multi-unit utility commitments, developers cannot secure low-cost project financing or scale up manufacturing, keeping projected power prices too high to attract the very orders needed to make SMRs commercially viable.

noweb.answer: The main bottleneck is financing the first commercial projects at a price utilities can justify. Without a track record of construction costs and schedules, utilities and lenders face a high risk of delays and cost overruns. Small modular reactors are expected to get cheaper through standardized factory production, but manufacturers need firm orders to reach that scale. Utilities, in turn, want proven costs before committing to large orders.

points.why: The response links the lack of a construction cost track record directly to overrun exposure on the first commercial projects.
quotes: Without a track record of construction costs and schedules, utilities and lenders face a high risk of delays and cost overruns.

points.why: Wanting proven costs before placing large orders does not establish that utilities strictly cap their financial exposure.
The response discusses manufacturers’ need for firm orders without addressing their ability to absorb construction overruns.
The response proposes neither multi-party risk sharing nor a federal backstop for residual overruns.

models.answer: The primary commercial bottleneck is cost uncertainty. Utilities need confidence that an SMR can be built on budget and sell electricity at a competitive price. Each reactor produces fewer megawatts over which to spread construction costs, so developers count on factory production and repeated builds of a standard design to bring costs down. That creates a financing dilemma: manufacturers need firm orders to justify investing in factories, while utilities hesitate to place those orders until early projects demonstrate reliable costs and construction schedules.

points.why: The response directly attributes utilities’ hesitation to uncertainty about whether early SMR projects can be built on budget.
quotes: The primary commercial bottleneck is cost uncertainty.
Utilities need confidence that an SMR can be built on budget
utilities hesitate to place those orders until early projects demonstrate reliable costs and construction schedules.

points.why: The response describes utilities delaying orders but gives no indication that they insist on capping their financial exposure.
The response discusses manufacturers’ need for firm orders to justify factory investment without addressing their capacity to absorb construction overruns.
The response proposes no arrangement for sharing capped risk among stakeholders with a federal backstop.
